chapters.title: Executive Brief
chapters.guidingQuestion: What should I understand in my first ten minutes?
chapters.headline: Meridian's leadership is aligned on the right problems but has not yet delivered against them, and several of the numbers used to justify investment — AI value, program completion, metric baselines — are not yet fully verifiable.
chapters.executive_synthesis: In the first ten minutes, three things matter. First, Meridian's economics are dual-engine — 60% provider, 40% health plan revenue, with 70% of plan revenue tied to Medicare Advantage/FFS — meaning Star Ratings and RAF accuracy act as revenue levers, not just compliance work, and a high-severity RAF evidence gap tied to Cotiviti directly threatens that priority. Second, leadership alignment is real: all 44 interviewed leaders raised the same core issues, yet execution lags, with the STARS 5.0 program only 8% complete. Third, the numbers behind the narrative need scrutiny before they're trusted: only 24% of the promised $63.8M in AI value is finance-validated, a third of tracked metrics lack usable baselines, 127 leadership statements contradict system-of-record evidence, and concentrated infrastructure risk sits in Epic and an unencrypted Corepoint interface. Together, these suggest a well-diagnosed organization whose evidence base still needs verification before further investment or board reporting.

key_insights.statement: Meridian's economics are dual-engine: 60% provider revenue and 40% health plan revenue, with 70% of plan revenue tied to Medicare Advantage/FFS — given this mix, Star Ratings and RAF accuracy could function as direct revenue levers rather than pure compliance overhead.

Epic represents a significant concentration point: it accounts for 17.4% of total vendor spend ($86.2M of $496.4M) supporting Clinical Informatics, and Epic Clarity — Test integrates with 82 other systems, making it a notable node in the integration graph.

Leadership is unusually aligned on the core diagnosis — value realization, investment priority, and capability gaps were raised by every one of 44 interviewed leaders — but that alignment has not yet translated into delivery, at least for the STARS 5.0 Improvement Program, which is only 8% complete.
The declared AI portfolio promises $63.8M of value but only $15.2M is finance-validated (24%), so AI benefit figures presented to the board should be treated as provisional.

A meaningful share of leadership testimony (127 of 996 responses) contradicts the documented system-of-record on the same topics, so leadership narrative and system evidence should be checked against each other before either is relied on alone.

tensions.statement: AI value realization confirmation is low ($15.2M finance-validated of $63.8M promised value, 24%), and value realization was raised by all 44 interviewed leaders as a shared topic of focus — a combination that could warrant closer scrutiny of how AI value is validated before further investment.

Metric infrastructure itself needs attention: 16 of 50 tracked metrics (roughly a third) lack a comparable baseline, target, or actual, and 18 of the remaining 34 mix notation between those fields, meaning performance claims on this portion of metrics are unsupported.

what_to_watch.statement: PHI exposure via an unencrypted legacy interface (Corepoint Integration Engine) is rated high severity, and Corepoint is also named across 2 separate risk/control entries, indicating concentrated exposure on aging integration infrastructure.
RAF evidence gap on suspect conditions is rated high severity and tied to Cotiviti, directly threatening the declared priority of reducing RAF evidence gaps.

questions_to_ask: Why is the Privileged Access Management Rollout still at 0% complete when the high-severity risk it is meant to close is already declared as directly impacting it?

AI value realization tracking shows $63.8M of promised value against $15.2M finance-validated — 24% confirmed. What is driving the gap between promised and validated value, and what would it take to close it?
Epic Community Connect Expansion is blocked because year-two funding is unconfirmed, despite being tied to the strategic priority of reducing interface sprawl — is year-two funding being pursued?

With the Databricks lakehouse target itself only at maturity level 1 of a target 2, is the modernization sequence (evaluate lakehouse, then migrate datamarts) realistic, or does it risk replacing one immature platform with another?

chapters.title: Our Business
chapters.guidingQuestion: How does this enterprise work and create value?
chapters.headline: Value is created through a vertically integrated model where 60% of revenue comes from owning care delivery (34 hospitals, 214 ambulatory sites) and 40% from an owned health plan whose economics hinge heavily on Medicare Advantage performance, all underpinned by a technology stack with concentrated vendor dependencies.
chapters.executive_synthesis: This enterprise creates value by owning both sides of care: provider operations across 34 hospitals and 214 ambulatory sites generate 60% of revenue, while an owned health plan contributes the remaining 40%. Within that health plan, 70% of revenue flows from Medicare Advantage and FFS, meaning Star Ratings and risk-adjustment accuracy function as direct economic levers, not just quality indicators. The model serves five distinct customer segments spanning Medicare, commercial, Medicaid, and self-pay populations, though whether these populations overlap across the plan and provider sides isn't established. Operationally, this value chain depends heavily on technology: more than half of the $960.8M technology budget goes to third-party contracts, with Epic alone representing 17.4% of vendor spend supporting clinical informatics. The systems underpinning the health plan's core economic levers—Cotiviti for risk-adjustment evidence and the HEDIS engine for quality measurement—carry flagged risk exposures, as does the Finance/GL Mart system, suggesting the mechanisms that translate care delivery into revenue are not without vulnerability.

key_insights.statement: Revenue is generated through a vertically integrated model spanning 34 hospitals, 214 ambulatory sites, and an owned health plan, with 60% of revenue from provider operations and 40% from the health plan.
Within the health plan, 70% of revenue comes from Medicare Advantage/FFS, making Star Rating and risk-adjustment accuracy direct economic levers rather than quality-only metrics.

Five customer segments are declared: Medicare Advantage members, Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries, commercial health plan members, Medicaid managed-care members, and self-pay/commercially insured patients across acute, ambulatory and behavioral health service lines. Whether these populations overlap across plan and provider revenue streams is not established by the facts, though the segment names suggest some populations could plausibly touch both.
Epic Systems represents 17.4% of total vendor spend ($86.2M of $496.4M), supporting Clinical Informatics via Epic Hyperspace, and this single-vendor dependency is flagged as a medium-severity risk.
Third-party contracted spend ($496.4M) is 52% of the total technology budget ($960.8M), meaning more than half of the technology budget is allocated to third-party contracts.

RAF evidence generation depends on the Cotiviti Quality Intelligence Platform, which carries a high-severity risk entry for evidence gaps on suspect conditions, while HEDIS numerator accuracy depends on the NCQA HEDIS Certified Measure Engine, which carries a medium-severity risk entry for abstraction-backlog undercounts. Separately, Finance/GL Mart (SQL Server On-Prem) shows a concentration of risk exposure with 4 open risk or control entries tied to that one system.

chapters.title: Strategy & Value Creation
chapters.guidingQuestion: Where are we trying to go, and what bets are we making?
chapters.headline: The strategy is a coherent set of high-conviction bets — Stars improvement, Community Connect, lakehouse consolidation, and governed AI — but every one of them is early-stage, underfunded or unconfirmed, and the portfolio's declared 1.14x return remains unvalidated.
chapters.executive_synthesis: The organization has named where it wants to go: a Medicare Advantage Star Rating of 4.5+ by 2028, consolidation of interface sprawl through Epic Community Connect, replacement of on-prem datamart sprawl with a Databricks lakehouse, and disciplined, human-in-the-loop AI adoption. These are real bets, not aspirations alone. But the evidence shows each is early and constrained: STARS improvement is 8% complete, Community Connect is 1% complete and blocked on unconfirmed funding, and the lakehouse initiative is still at evaluation with lock-in risk unassessed. Governance, meant to make the AI bet safe, is already pausing two of eighteen use cases and is flagged by 41 of 44 leaders as a friction point — a possible sign the safeguard is constraining throughput. Even automation opportunities rated highly, like interface failure triage, remain barely realized. Across the priority set, execution lags conviction, and the portfolio's headline 1.14x return on $739.7M is self-declared, not yet finance-confirmed — echoing a similar validation gap already seen in AI value claims.

key_insights.statement: Management has declared a strategic priority to lift the Medicare Advantage overall Star Rating from 3.5 to 4.5+ stars by measurement year 2028; the associated STARS 5.0 Improvement Program is currently only 8% complete.
Management is pursuing Epic Community Connect expansion to affiliated practices to reduce interface sprawl, but the program is 1% complete and blocked because year-two funding is unconfirmed.

Management has only reached evaluation stage on replacing the on-prem SQL Server datamart sprawl with a Databricks lakehouse, with the associated program at 12% completion and lock-in risk not yet assessed.

AI use cases are being deliberately governed with human-in-the-loop review, yet two of 18 declared use cases are already paused pending governance review, suggesting the governance bet is actively constraining rollout, not just theoretical.

tensions.statement: Leadership consensus names governance friction as a near-universal concern (41 of 44 leaders), coinciding with a declared strategic priority to govern AI use cases with human-in-the-loop review as they move from concept to pilot. This raises the possibility that the governance model intended to reduce risk is itself being perceived as a throughput constraint, though the two facts alone do not confirm a direct causal link.

Interface Failure Alert Triage is rated a "High" automation candidate but sits at only 6% automation with a 6% error rate, suggesting a gap between recognized automation opportunity and realized capability for this process.

The declared portfolio shows $739.7M of budget against $845.9M of expected value (a 1.14x declared return) across 38 programs, self-declared and not yet finance-confirmed. This unvalidated status echoes the AI portfolio, where only 24% of promised value ($15.2M of $63.8M) has been finance-validated so far, though the confirmation rate for the 38-program portfolio itself is not yet known.

Programs directly tied to declared strategic priorities (STARS, RAF, Community Connect, SQL sprawl) are all in the low single-to-low-double-digit percent complete range, suggesting the transformation load exceeds current execution capacity across the priority set, not just one program.

questions_to_ask: AI value realization tracking shows $63.8M of promised value against $15.2M finance-validated — 24% confirmed. What is driving the gap between promised and validated value, and what would it take to close it?
Epic Community Connect Expansion is blocked because year-two funding is unconfirmed, despite being tied to the strategic priority of reducing interface sprawl — is year-two funding being pursued?

chapters.title: How We Operate
chapters.guidingQuestion: How is the enterprise organized and how does work get done?
chapters.headline: The enterprise's operating rhythm cannot yet be verified through its own metrics, since half of tracked performance measures suffer from inconsistent or missing baseline/target/actual data.
chapters.executive_synthesis: A clear picture of how work actually gets done depends on being able to trust the metrics used to track it, and that trust is currently only partial. Of the 50 performance metrics tracked, 34 have a comparable baseline, target, and actual figure, but 18 of those mix inconsistent notation across the three fields, undermining confidence in direct comparison. The remaining 16 metrics lack a comparable baseline, target, and actual entirely, meaning any performance claims tied to them cannot currently be trusted at face value. This does not tell us how the organization is structured or how workflows move through it, but it does establish an important limit: operational performance, as currently measured, is only reliably assessable for a minority of tracked metrics. Until notation is standardized and missing baselines are filled in, statements about operational effectiveness drawn from this metric set should be treated cautiously rather than as settled fact.

key_insights.statement: 34 of 50 tracked performance metrics have a comparable baseline/target/actual, but 18 of those mix inconsistent notation between the fields, and the remaining 16 metrics lack a comparable baseline/target/actual entirely, so metric-level performance claims for those 16 cannot currently be trusted at face value.

chapters.title: Technology & Data
chapters.guidingQuestion: What enables the business, and where is complexity or dependency concentrated?
chapters.headline: Epic Clarity anchors reporting as the single most-connected system while sitting a full level below its architecture target, making it the clearest concentration of both operational dependency and modernization risk in the technology estate.
chapters.executive_synthesis: What enables the business today is a data and analytics estate built around Epic Clarity, the most-integrated system with 82 connections, but it operates below its architecture maturity target — a gap echoed across the on-prem SQL Server datamart, SSIS/SSAS/SSRS ETL estate, Tableau Server, and even the proposed Databricks lakehouse replacement, none of which yet decisively clears its target. Complexity is compounded by scale and sensitivity: 72% of tracked data assets carry regulated data, yet all 27 declared evidence sources remain unapproved for loading, suggesting governance for Star Rating and RAF-critical analytics is still early-stage. Dependency risk extends beyond software — critical infrastructure such as the Marsh Point server room and VMware compute cluster have thin capacity headroom, constraining how fast new initiatives can be layered on. Financially, 19% of the application estate ($52.2M) is already flagged for replacement, and none of 72 vendor contracts have document-level evidence, limiting visibility into pricing and renewal exposure. Together these point to concentrated, thinly governed dependency rather than a modernized foundation.

key_insights.statement: Epic Clarity's position as the most-integrated system (82 connections) combined with its below-target architecture maturity (level 3 of 4) suggests it could be a single point of both operational dependency and modernization risk across whatever reporting functions rely on it.

The on-prem SQL Server datamart estate, SSIS/SSAS/SSRS ETL/cube estate, and Tableau Server are each one point below their respective maturity targets (2 of 3, 2 of 3, and 2 of 3), while the proposed Databricks lakehouse replacement is evaluated at maturity level 1 against a target of 2 on AI/ML Capability. Though these scores span different dimensions (architecture/scalability, analytics, and AI/ML) and aren't directly comparable, the gap-to-target pattern is similar across the current estate and its proposed replacement, suggesting the modernization target may not yet represent a decisively more mature state.
376 of 520 tracked data assets/integrations (about 72%) carry regulated data, indicating that most of the tracked estate is compliance-sensitive.

27 of 27 declared evidence sources are not yet approved for loading, which could suggest the analytics foundation intended to support Star Rating and RAF decision-making is still in an early stage of governance.

tensions.statement: 57 applications (19% of the estate, $52.2M) are already flagged as replacement candidates, which could represent a significant baseline cost tied to the existing estate before any new investment.

Core data platforms show maturity gaps against their targets: Epic Clarity's Platform Architecture & Scalability sits at level 3 of a target 4, on-prem datamarts' Platform Architecture & Scalability at 2 of a target 3, and the Databricks lakehouse's AI/ML Capability at only level 1 of a target 2.

Critical infrastructure has thin capacity headroom — Marsh Point Regional Server Room (tier2-critical) at 8% and VMware compute cluster (tier1-critical) at 14% — which could constrain the pace at which new digital and analytics initiatives can be layered on.
None of 72 declared vendor contracts have document-level evidence behind them, limiting management's ability to interrogate pricing, SLA, or renewal exposure at the enterprise level.

questions_to_ask: With the Databricks lakehouse target itself only at maturity level 1 of a target 2, is the modernization sequence (evaluate lakehouse, then migrate datamarts) realistic, or does it risk replacing one immature platform with another?

chapters.title: Performance & Value
chapters.guidingQuestion: Are we moving toward outcomes, and can we prove the value?
chapters.headline: The portfolio is not yet proving value: only 24% of promised AI benefit is finance-validated, adoption of flagship AI tools lags targets by roughly 50 points, and a third of tracked metrics can't even support a verdict.
chapters.executive_synthesis: The evidence does not yet show a confirmed shift toward outcomes. Flagship AI tools are far below adoption targets, and priority programs like STARS, RAF, and Community Connect remain in single-to-low-double-digit completion. Of the $63.8M in promised AI value, only $15.2M (24%) has been finance-validated — a gap echoed at the portfolio level, where the declared 1.14x expected-value-to-budget ratio across 38 programs is self-declared, not finance-confirmed. Structural measurement gaps compound the problem: 16 of 50 tracked metrics lack a usable baseline/target/actual, and 18 more mix notation, leaving a third of the metric portfolio unable to support a performance verdict. Contract-level evidence is similarly absent, with zero of 72 vendor contracts supporting document-level assessment. The CEO's own account of an unverified benefit case, and Finance's testimony that it has never signed off on a baseline or cohort definition, reinforce a recurring theme across leadership: benefit claims are being made faster than they can be validated. Whether this is systemic or incidental remains unestablished, but proof of value is currently lacking.

key_insights.statement: AI adoption is materially below target for flagship tools: Sepsis Early-Warning Model is 52.8 points below its adoption target and STARS Member Outreach Next-Best-Action is 47.7 points below target.
Only 24% of promised AI value ($15.2M of $63.8M) is finance-validated, and priority-linked programs (STARS, RAF, Community Connect) are all in single-digit-to-low-double-digit percent completion.
16 of 50 tracked metrics lack a comparable baseline/target/actual, and 18 more mix notation, meaning a third of the metric portfolio cannot currently support a performance verdict either way.
No vendor contracts (0 of 72) have document-level evidence extraction, so contract performance (pricing, SLA compliance) cannot currently be assessed at the enterprise level.

tensions.statement: The CEO's own testimony that Actuarial & Underwriting Analytics Modernization was approved with a benefit number nobody has since verified is a concrete example of the value-realization theme that was raised, in some form, by all 44 interviewed leaders.

The declared portfolio's 1.14x expected-value-to-budget ratio ($845.9M vs $739.7M across 38 programs) is self-declared and not finance-confirmed — the same caveat that applies to the AI value figures ($63.8M promised vs $15.2M finance-validated, 24% confirmed). These are two separate instances of unconfirmed benefit cases; whether they reflect a broader pattern across the wider portfolio is not established by these figures alone but may warrant further validation.

VP Finance Operations testimony that Finance has never been given a baseline or cohort definition it would sign off on suggests a persistent gap between program benefit claims and finance validation capability, though whether this reflects a structural pattern or an incidental lapse isn't established by this statement alone.

chapters.title: Leadership Perspective
chapters.guidingQuestion: What do leaders agree on, disagree on, and worry about?
chapters.headline: Leadership is nearly unanimous that value realization, investment priority, and capability gaps are unresolved, but perception diverges from documented system state in roughly one in eight cases.
chapters.executive_synthesis: Across all 44 interviewed leaders, consensus is striking: every one raised value realization, investment priority, and capability gap as live concerns, suggesting shared unease that ambition is outrunning resources and skills. Near-consensus extends to vendor dependency and data trust (36 of 44 each), grounded in concrete testimony like an eight-week vendor queue and a CEO who keeps personal data extracts rather than trust reported numbers, and to governance friction (41 of 44), epitomized by a six-week architecture review process leaders call sensible in standard but broken in practice. Disagreement, where it exists, is narrow rather than sharp: ai_governance and finance_evidence were each flagged by only a single leader, meaning these are isolated observations rather than shared worries, and leadership has not yet converged on them. Underlying all of this is a caution about the reliability of leadership perception itself: 127 of 996 interview responses contradict system-of-record evidence, showing that what leaders believe and what systems document diverge in a material minority of cases.

key_insights.statement: All 44 interviewed leaders raised value realization as a concern, indicating a strong consensus among them about whether investments are delivering claimed benefit.

All 44 interviewed leaders raised both investment priority and capability gap, indicating broad consensus that these are top-of-mind issues; this pattern is consistent with, though does not itself confirm, a view that resources and skills are misaligned to ambition.

36 of 44 leaders raised vendor dependency and 36 raised data trust as concerns, both echoed in specific testimony (e.g., the CFO's comment on Zelis Healthcare's eight-week queue, the CEO's comment on keeping personal data extracts rather than trusting reported numbers).
Governance friction was raised by 41 of 44 leaders, with the CEO specifically characterizing architecture review as adding six weeks with standards that are sensible but a process that is not.

tensions.statement: While enterprise-wide themes are near-universal, ai_governance and finance_evidence were each raised by only a single leader, indicating these are not shared concerns but isolated observations (from a VP Finance Operations, on the absence of an agreed finance baseline) that leadership as a whole has not yet converged on.

127 of 996 leadership interview responses contradict the system-of-record evidence on the same topic, indicating leadership perception and documented system state diverge in a material minority of cases.

chapters.title: What Needs Attention
chapters.guidingQuestion: What tensions, risks, dependencies and decisions deserve executive attention?
chapters.headline: Executive attention should concentrate on four converging exposures — unvalidated AI value claims, unreliable metric infrastructure, aging integration and migration risk, and thin infrastructure headroom — each rated high severity or material enough to warrant decision-level scrutiny before further investment or reliance.
chapters.executive_synthesis: The clearest signal for executive attention is a validation gap: only 24% of promised AI value has been finance-confirmed, yet all 44 interviewed leaders flagged value realization as a shared concern, suggesting further AI investment should be paired with tighter proof requirements. That concern is compounded by the state of the metrics themselves — a third lack basic baseline, target, or actual data, and over half of the remainder mix notation, meaning many performance claims across the organization cannot currently be trusted at face value. Infrastructure and migration risks add further urgency: an unencrypted legacy interface (Corepoint) presents high-severity PHI exposure and recurs across multiple risk entries, a high-severity RAF evidence gap tied to Cotiviti threatens a declared reduction priority, and the Cerner-to-Epic migration at St. Anselm remains high-risk with its decommission only 10% complete. Separately, a tier2-critical server room operating with just 8% capacity headroom and backup-only disaster recovery raises continuity questions disproportionate to its designated importance. Together these form a set of dependencies and open exposures warranting near-term decisions.

key_insights.statement: AI value realization confirmation is low ($15.2M finance-validated of $63.8M promised value, 24%), and value realization was raised by all 44 interviewed leaders as a shared topic of focus — a combination that could warrant closer scrutiny of how AI value is validated before further investment.

Metric infrastructure itself needs attention: 16 of 50 tracked metrics (roughly a third) lack a comparable baseline, target, or actual, and 18 of the remaining 34 mix notation between those fields, meaning performance claims on this portion of metrics are unsupported.

tensions.statement: PHI exposure via an unencrypted legacy interface (Corepoint Integration Engine) is rated high severity, and Corepoint is also named across 2 separate risk/control entries, indicating concentrated exposure on aging integration infrastructure.
RAF evidence gap on suspect conditions is rated high severity and tied to Cotiviti, directly threatening the declared priority of reducing RAF evidence gaps.

The Cerner-to-Epic data migration integrity risk at St. Anselm is rated high severity while the associated decommission program is only 10% complete, leaving the exposure window open for an extended period.
Marsh Point Regional Server Room is tier2-critical but has only 8% capacity headroom and a backup-only DR tier, a combination that could pose continuity risk given its critical designation.

publishedGeneration.enterprise_story: Meridian's economics run on a single connected model: 60% of revenue comes from owned providers and 40% from its health plan, itself 70% Medicare Advantage/FFS, tying clinical delivery and payer economics together. The technology estate shows a matching concentration — Epic accounts for 17.4% of vendor spend ($86.2M of $496.4M) and Epic Clarity sits at the center of the integration graph with 82 connections, a level of connectivity suggesting clinical, quality, and actuarial data may share common infrastructure, though the specific systems and data types involved aren't confirmed. Leadership is unusually unified on the diagnosis: value realization, investment priority, and capability gap were each raised by all 44 interviewed leaders. Yet that consensus has not yet translated into delivery — the STARS 5.0 and RAF Capture Modernization programs most tied to declared strategic priorities are only 8% and 3% complete, and of the $63.8M in promised AI value, only $15.2M (24%) is finance-validated. Together these point to a gap between strategic intent and the organization's demonstrated capacity to deliver against it.

AI value tracking shows only 24% of promised value ($15.2M of $63.8M) is finance-validated, indicating an investment/outcome gap in the AI portfolio.

value_creation_model.summary: Meridian's revenue comes from a vertically integrated model spanning 34 hospitals, 214 ambulatory sites, and an owned health plan, with 60% of revenue from provider operations and 40% from the health plan. Within the health plan, 70% of revenue comes from Medicare Advantage/FFS, which makes Star Rating and risk-adjustment accuracy direct economic levers rather than quality-only metrics. Five customer segments are declared — Medicare Advantage members, Medicare FFS beneficiaries, commercial health plan members, Medicaid managed-care members, and self-pay/commercially insured patients across acute, ambulatory, and behavioral health lines — though whether these populations overlap across plan and provider revenue streams isn't established, even if the segment names suggest some plausibly touch both. Supporting evidence generation for these metrics carries its own risks: the Cotiviti Quality Intelligence Platform, which underpins RAF evidence, has a high-severity risk entry for evidence gaps on suspect conditions, while the NCQA HEDIS Certified Measure Engine carries a medium-severity risk for abstraction-backlog undercounts, and Finance/GL Mart (SQL Server On-Prem) shows a concentration of risk with four open entries tied to that single system. Epic Systems, which supports Clinical Informatics via Epic Hyperspace, represents 17.4% of total vendor spend ($86.2M of $496.4M) and is flagged as a medium-severity single-vendor dependency risk. More broadly, third-party contracted spend of $496.4M makes up 52% of the total $960.8M technology budget, meaning more than half of the technology budget goes to third-party contracts.

primary_value_drivers.statement: Revenue is generated through a vertically integrated model spanning 34 hospitals, 214 ambulatory sites, and an owned health plan, with 60% of revenue from provider operations and 40% from the health plan.

economic_dependencies.statement: Epic Systems represents 17.4% of total vendor spend ($86.2M of $496.4M), supporting Clinical Informatics via Epic Hyperspace, and this single-vendor dependency is flagged as a medium-severity risk.

RAF evidence generation depends on the Cotiviti Quality Intelligence Platform, which carries a high-severity risk entry for evidence gaps on suspect conditions, while HEDIS numerator accuracy depends on the NCQA HEDIS Certified Measure Engine, which carries a medium-severity risk entry for abstraction-backlog undercounts. Separately, Finance/GL Mart (SQL Server On-Prem) shows a concentration of risk exposure with 4 open risk or control entries tied to that one system.

strategic_bets.statement: Management has declared a strategic priority to lift the Medicare Advantage overall Star Rating from 3.5 to 4.5+ stars by measurement year 2028; the associated STARS 5.0 Improvement Program is currently only 8% complete.
Management is pursuing Epic Community Connect expansion to affiliated practices to reduce interface sprawl, but the program is 1% complete and blocked because year-two funding is unconfirmed.

Management has only reached evaluation stage on replacing the on-prem SQL Server datamart sprawl with a Databricks lakehouse, with the associated program at 12% completion and lock-in risk not yet assessed.

AI use cases are being deliberately governed with human-in-the-loop review, yet two of 18 declared use cases are already paused pending governance review, suggesting the governance bet is actively constraining rollout, not just theoretical.

structural_constraints.statement: 57 applications (19% of the estate, $52.2M) are already flagged as replacement candidates, which could represent a significant baseline cost tied to the existing estate before any new investment.

Core data platforms show maturity gaps against their targets: Epic Clarity's Platform Architecture & Scalability sits at level 3 of a target 4, on-prem datamarts' Platform Architecture & Scalability at 2 of a target 3, and the Databricks lakehouse's AI/ML Capability at only level 1 of a target 2.

Critical infrastructure has thin capacity headroom — Marsh Point Regional Server Room (tier2-critical) at 8% and VMware compute cluster (tier1-critical) at 14% — which could constrain the pace at which new digital and analytics initiatives can be layered on.
None of 72 declared vendor contracts have document-level evidence behind them, limiting management's ability to interrogate pricing, SLA, or renewal exposure at the enterprise level.

34 of 50 tracked performance metrics have a comparable baseline/target/actual, but 18 of those mix inconsistent notation between the fields, and the remaining 16 metrics lack a comparable baseline/target/actual entirely, so metric-level performance claims for those 16 cannot currently be trusted at face value.

operating_tensions.statement: Leadership consensus names governance friction as a near-universal concern (41 of 44 leaders), coinciding with a declared strategic priority to govern AI use cases with human-in-the-loop review as they move from concept to pilot. This raises the possibility that the governance model intended to reduce risk is itself being perceived as a throughput constraint, though the two facts alone do not confirm a direct causal link.

Interface Failure Alert Triage is rated a "High" automation candidate but sits at only 6% automation with a 6% error rate, suggesting a gap between recognized automation opportunity and realized capability for this process.

The declared portfolio shows $739.7M of budget against $845.9M of expected value (a 1.14x declared return) across 38 programs, self-declared and not yet finance-confirmed. This unvalidated status echoes the AI portfolio, where only 24% of promised value ($15.2M of $63.8M) has been finance-validated so far, though the confirmation rate for the 38-program portfolio itself is not yet known.

Programs directly tied to declared strategic priorities (STARS, RAF, Community Connect, SQL sprawl) are all in the low single-to-low-double-digit percent complete range, suggesting the transformation load exceeds current execution capacity across the priority set, not just one program.

leadership_consensus.statement: All 44 interviewed leaders raised value realization as a concern, indicating a strong consensus among them about whether investments are delivering claimed benefit.

All 44 interviewed leaders raised both investment priority and capability gap, indicating broad consensus that these are top-of-mind issues; this pattern is consistent with, though does not itself confirm, a view that resources and skills are misaligned to ambition.

36 of 44 leaders raised vendor dependency and 36 raised data trust as concerns, both echoed in specific testimony (e.g., the CFO's comment on Zelis Healthcare's eight-week queue, the CEO's comment on keeping personal data extracts rather than trusting reported numbers).
Governance friction was raised by 41 of 44 leaders, with the CEO specifically characterizing architecture review as adding six weeks with standards that are sensible but a process that is not.

leadership_disagreements.statement: While enterprise-wide themes are near-universal, ai_governance and finance_evidence were each raised by only a single leader, indicating these are not shared concerns but isolated observations (from a VP Finance Operations, on the absence of an agreed finance baseline) that leadership as a whole has not yet converged on.

127 of 996 leadership interview responses contradict the system-of-record evidence on the same topic, indicating leadership perception and documented system state diverge in a material minority of cases.

technology_and_data_implications.statement: Epic Clarity's position as the most-integrated system (82 connections) combined with its below-target architecture maturity (level 3 of 4) suggests it could be a single point of both operational dependency and modernization risk across whatever reporting functions rely on it.

The on-prem SQL Server datamart estate, SSIS/SSAS/SSRS ETL/cube estate, and Tableau Server are each one point below their respective maturity targets (2 of 3, 2 of 3, and 2 of 3), while the proposed Databricks lakehouse replacement is evaluated at maturity level 1 against a target of 2 on AI/ML Capability. Though these scores span different dimensions (architecture/scalability, analytics, and AI/ML) and aren't directly comparable, the gap-to-target pattern is similar across the current estate and its proposed replacement, suggesting the modernization target may not yet represent a decisively more mature state.
376 of 520 tracked data assets/integrations (about 72%) carry regulated data, indicating that most of the tracked estate is compliance-sensitive.

27 of 27 declared evidence sources are not yet approved for loading, which could suggest the analytics foundation intended to support Star Rating and RAF decision-making is still in an early stage of governance.

material_risks.statement: PHI exposure via an unencrypted legacy interface (Corepoint Integration Engine) is rated high severity, and Corepoint is also named across 2 separate risk/control entries, indicating concentrated exposure on aging integration infrastructure.
RAF evidence gap on suspect conditions is rated high severity and tied to Cotiviti, directly threatening the declared priority of reducing RAF evidence gaps.

The Cerner-to-Epic data migration integrity risk at St. Anselm is rated high severity while the associated decommission program is only 10% complete, leaving the exposure window open for an extended period.
Marsh Point Regional Server Room is tier2-critical but has only 8% capacity headroom and a backup-only DR tier, a combination that could pose continuity risk given its critical designation.

value_realization_tensions.statement: The CEO's own testimony that Actuarial & Underwriting Analytics Modernization was approved with a benefit number nobody has since verified is a concrete example of the value-realization theme that was raised, in some form, by all 44 interviewed leaders.

The declared portfolio's 1.14x expected-value-to-budget ratio ($845.9M vs $739.7M across 38 programs) is self-declared and not finance-confirmed — the same caveat that applies to the AI value figures ($63.8M promised vs $15.2M finance-validated, 24% confirmed). These are two separate instances of unconfirmed benefit cases; whether they reflect a broader pattern across the wider portfolio is not established by these figures alone but may warrant further validation.

VP Finance Operations testimony that Finance has never been given a baseline or cohort definition it would sign off on suggests a persistent gap between program benefit claims and finance validation capability, though whether this reflects a structural pattern or an incidental lapse isn't established by this statement alone.

what_needs_attention.statement: AI value realization confirmation is low ($15.2M finance-validated of $63.8M promised value, 24%), and value realization was raised by all 44 interviewed leaders as a shared topic of focus — a combination that could warrant closer scrutiny of how AI value is validated before further investment.

Metric infrastructure itself needs attention: 16 of 50 tracked metrics (roughly a third) lack a comparable baseline, target, or actual, and 18 of the remaining 34 mix notation between those fields, meaning performance claims on this portion of metrics are unsupported.

Epic represents a significant concentration point: it accounts for 17.4% of total vendor spend ($86.2M of $496.4M) supporting Clinical Informatics, and Epic Clarity — Test integrates with 82 other systems, making it a notable node in the integration graph.

Leadership is unusually aligned on the core diagnosis — value realization, investment priority, and capability gaps were raised by every one of 44 interviewed leaders — but that alignment has not yet translated into delivery, at least for the STARS 5.0 Improvement Program, which is only 8% complete.

A meaningful share of leadership testimony (127 of 996 responses) contradicts the documented system-of-record on the same topics, so leadership narrative and system evidence should be checked against each other before either is relied on alone.

The facts support the spend percentage and medium-severity single-vendor risk, but characterizing the entire business model as 'depending on' this and adding 'financial core' scope beyond Clinical Informatics/Hyperspace is unsupported broadening.
The fact only states the percentage figure; interpreting this as meaning enablement is 'externally sourced rather than owned' adds an interpretive claim about ownership not stated in the facts.

The facts don't establish that Finance/GL Mart is tied to RAF/HEDIS evidence generation, nor that Cotiviti or NCQA engine each carry 'multiple' open risk entries—only Finance/GL Mart has 4, while the others each have one entry cited.
